candidates.label: Double density at the right heart border
Left ventricular enlargement (apex displaced down and out)

items.concept: valvular heart disease; mitral stenosis; left atrial enlargement; pulmonary venous hypertension
items.explanation: Look first at the heart size and the left heart border: a normal cardiothoracic ratio with a straight left border, a double density and a splayed carina says 'big left atrium, normal left ventricle'. Add signs of pulmonary venous hypertension (upper lobe diversion, Kerley B lines) and the film reads as mitral stenosis. On the lateral film the enlarged left atrium bulges backward and indents or displaces the barium-filled oesophagus posteriorly. Late films may show pulmonary haemosiderosis, small ossified nodules, or calcification of the mitral valve or left atrial wall. Associated findings: loud S1, opening snap and a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble with presystolic accentuation in sinus rhythm; ECG with P mitrale or atrial fibrillation, and right axis deviation with RV hypertrophy once pulmonary hypertension develops; echo shows a doming valve with commissural fusion and an MVA by planimetry or 220/PHT (severe at 1.5 cm2 or less). What would change the picture: an enlarged left ventricle together with the large left atrium favours chronic mitral regurgitation; a large pulmonary artery with plethora and no left atrial enlargement favours an atrial septal defect.

findings.label: Splayed carina (widened carinal angle)
findings.why: The left atrium lies directly below the carina. As it enlarges behind a fixed, narrowed mitral orifice it pushes the left main bronchus upward, so the carinal angle opens beyond about 90 degrees.

findings.label: Double density at the right heart border
findings.why: The left atrium is a posterior chamber. When it enlarges to the right it projects through the right atrial shadow as a second, denser curved contour inside (or, when very large, beyond) the right heart border.

findings.label: Straightened left heart border
findings.why: The enlarged left atrial appendage, helped by a prominent main pulmonary artery when pulmonary hypertension develops, fills the normal concavity (cardiac waist) between the pulmonary artery and the left ventricle, so the left border runs straight: the 'mitralised' heart.

findings.label: Kerley B (septal) lines
findings.why: Short (under 2 cm) horizontal lines that meet the lateral pleura at both bases are interlobular septa thickened by interstitial fluid and distended lymphatics. A chronically raised left atrial pressure keeps them oedematous; in long-standing MS they can become fibrotic and persist.

findings.label: Upper lobe venous diversion (cephalisation)
findings.why: In the erect patient lower-zone vessels are normally larger (gravity). With raised pulmonary venous pressure, perivascular oedema and hypoxic vasoconstriction in the lower zones send flow upward, so upper-zone vessels become as large as or larger than lower-zone vessels.

links.why: A fixed mitral obstruction loads the left atrium while the left ventricle stays small: a large left atrium with a normal-sized LV points to MS rather than MR.
A double density means marked left atrial enlargement, which with a normal LV is most often rheumatic mitral stenosis.
Left atrial appendage enlargement is typical of rheumatic MS; added pulmonary artery prominence from secondary pulmonary hypertension straightens the border further.
The transmitral gradient raises left atrial, pulmonary venous and capillary pressure; septal oedema is the interstitial stage of that venous hypertension.
Upper lobe diversion is the earliest radiographic sign of pulmonary venous hypertension, here caused by the stenotic mitral valve.

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; mitral valve disease); Felson's Principles of Chest Roentgenology; ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines
items.title: Rheumatic mitral stenosis

candidates.label: Peripheral pruning of the pulmonary arteries

items.concept: heart failure; acute pulmonary oedema; pulmonary venous hypertension
items.explanation: Look first at the hila and the lung bases, then run the heart failure checklist ABCDE: Alveolar (bat-wing) oedema, Kerley B lines, Cardiomegaly, Dilated upper lobe vessels, Effusions. Four are present; the heart size is normal, which is common when oedema is acute (acute MI, acute severe MR, hypertensive crisis, rapid atrial fibrillation) because the LV has had no time to dilate. As a rough guide, upper lobe diversion appears at a wedge pressure of about 13-18 mmHg, interstitial oedema at about 18-25 mmHg and alveolar oedema above about 25 mmHg; the film lags behind the haemodynamics by hours on the way in and by a day or more on the way out. Associated: orthopnoea, tachypnoea, bilateral crackles, S3, raised JVP; ECG for ischaemia or arrhythmia; troponin and natriuretic peptides; echo for LV function and acute valve lesions. What would change the picture: patchy peripheral opacities with a normal vascular pedicle and no septal lines or effusion favour ARDS; a single lobar opacity with air bronchograms favours pneumonia.

findings.label: Bat-wing perihilar alveolar opacities
findings.why: When capillary pressure rises well above plasma oncotic pressure, fluid floods the alveoli. It collects around the hila first and the outer cortex is relatively spared (thought to reflect better lymphatic drainage and respiratory pumping at the periphery), giving bilateral, roughly symmetric perihilar opacities shaped like bat wings.

findings.label: Kerley B (septal) lines
findings.why: Interstitial oedema thickens the interlobular septa at both lung bases; they appear as short horizontal lines that meet the lateral pleura. This interstitial stage usually precedes alveolar flooding.

findings.label: Right pleural effusion
findings.why: Raised venous pressure pushes a transudate into the pleural space, blunting the costophrenic angle with a meniscus. In heart failure effusions are usually bilateral or right-sided; an isolated large left effusion should prompt a search for another cause.

findings.label: Upper lobe venous diversion (cephalisation)
findings.why: Upper-zone vessels as large as or larger than lower-zone vessels, with hazy, indistinct hila, show raised pulmonary venous pressure: the first stage of the sequence diversion, interstitial oedema, alveolar oedema.

links.why: Perihilar alveolar oedema with septal lines, effusion and upper lobe diversion is hydrostatic (cardiogenic) oedema; ARDS gives patchy, often peripheral opacities without septal lines or effusions.
Septal lines are the interstitial stage of hydrostatic oedema from a raised left atrial (wedge) pressure.

A transudative effusion from raised venous pressure belongs to the congestive picture; it is uncommon in ARDS, and in pneumonia an effusion sits on the side of the consolidation rather than with septal lines and upper lobe diversion.
Upper lobe diversion places the problem on the venous (post-capillary) side: the left heart is not emptying.

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; acute heart failure); Felson's Principles of Chest Roentgenology; ESC 2021 heart failure guidelines and 2023 focused update
items.title: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema

candidates.label: Dilated ascending aorta (right upper mediastinal bulge)
Double density at the right heart border

items.explanation: Look first at the heart size: CTR above 0.5 on an erect PA film (an AP or supine film magnifies the heart, so do not call cardiomegaly from it). Then look at the lungs: congestion and an effusion say the large heart is failing. Associated: displaced apex, S3 gallop, functional mitral regurgitation murmur; ECG often LBBB, poor R wave progression, low limb lead voltage or atrial fibrillation; echo shows a dilated LV with global systolic dysfunction not explained by coronary disease or abnormal loading, then the cause is sought (genetic, myocarditis, alcohol, peripartum, tachycardia, toxic). What would change the picture: a globular, sharply outlined silhouette with clear lungs favours a large pericardial effusion; a normal-sized heart with calcified pericardium, pleural effusions and relatively clear lungs favours constriction; a large left atrium with a normal LV favours mitral stenosis.

findings.label: Cardiomegaly (CTR > 0.5)
findings.why: The transverse cardiac diameter is more than half the internal thoracic diameter on a PA film (CTR about 0.66 here). A dilated, poorly contracting LV makes the silhouette large and globular, with the apex displaced down and to the left.

findings.label: Right pleural effusion
findings.why: Fluid with a meniscus hides the right costophrenic angle and dome: a transudate from raised venous pressure. Heart failure effusions are usually bilateral or right-sided.

findings.label: Upper lobe venous diversion (cephalisation)
findings.why: Distended upper-zone vessels and hazy hila show a raised LV filling pressure transmitted back to the pulmonary veins.

links.why: A dilated LV is the usual reason for a CTR well above 0.5 with an apex displaced down and out.
Effusion is the 'E' of the heart failure checklist: raised systemic and pulmonary venous pressure in a failing heart.
Venous congestion shows the large heart has a high filling pressure; a large pericardial effusion usually leaves the lungs clear.

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; dilated cardiomyopathy); Felson's Principles of Chest Roentgenology; ESC 2023 cardiomyopathy guidelines; ESC 2021 heart failure guidelines
items.title: Dilated cardiomyopathy with congestive heart failure

items.concept: cyanotic congenital heart disease; decreased pulmonary blood flow
items.explanation: Look first at the pulmonary vascularity (more or less than normal), then at the heart size and shape. A cyanotic patient with dark lungs and a normal-sized boot-shaped heart has tetralogy of Fallot until proven otherwise. A right-sided aortic arch occurs in about a quarter of cases (this film has a left arch). Associated: cyanosis, clubbing, squatting and hypercyanotic spells; a harsh ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal border from the RV outflow (the large VSD itself is silent; the murmur shortens or disappears in a spell); single S2; ECG with right axis deviation and RV hypertrophy; echo shows a large malaligned VSD, an overriding aorta and RV outflow or pulmonary valve stenosis. What would change the picture: oligaemia with a huge box-shaped heart suggests Ebstein anomaly; plethora with a narrow pedicle and an oval heart suggests transposition; plethora with a large pulmonary artery suggests a left-to-right shunt such as a VSD.

findings.label: Boot-shaped heart (coeur en sabot)
findings.why: RV hypertrophy turns the apex upward and outward, and the small RV outflow tract and pulmonary trunk leave a concave pulmonary segment (the pulmonary bay), so the outline looks like a boot. The heart is usually not enlarged: the RV is pressure loaded (hypertrophy), not volume loaded, and decompresses through the large VSD.

findings.label: Oligaemic lung fields (reduced vascularity)
findings.why: RV outflow obstruction diverts blood right-to-left across the VSD into the aorta, so pulmonary blood flow falls: small hila and thin, sparse vessels in dark lung fields.

links.why: RV hypertrophy with a hypoplastic RV outflow and pulmonary trunk is the anatomy of tetralogy (RV outflow obstruction, VSD, overriding aorta, RV hypertrophy).
Reduced pulmonary flow from RV outflow obstruction with a right-to-left shunt across the VSD; plethora would argue against tetralogy.

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; congenital heart disease); Perloff's Clinical Recognition of Congenital Heart Disease; ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines
items.title: Tetralogy of Fallot

items.concept: cyanotic congenital heart disease; increased pulmonary blood flow
items.explanation: Look first at the superior mediastinum and the vascularity. A cyanotic newborn with a narrow pedicle, an oval heart and increased pulmonary vascularity has d-TGA. The film is often normal in the first days of life; the classic shape develops over the first weeks. Associated: marked cyanosis with little respiratory distress and a poor rise in oxygen saturation on 100% oxygen (the two circulations run in parallel); single loud S2 from the anterior aorta; ECG often normal for age; echo shows the aorta arising from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV, running parallel in the parasternal long axis. Newborn management: prostaglandin E1 to keep the duct open, balloon atrial septostomy when mixing is poor, then the arterial switch operation. What would change the picture: a widened 'snowman' upper mediastinum with plethora suggests supracardiac TAPVR; oligaemia with a boot-shaped heart suggests tetralogy; a huge box-shaped heart with oligaemia suggests Ebstein anomaly.

findings.label: Egg-on-a-string cardiac silhouette
findings.why: The aorta lies in front of the pulmonary artery instead of beside it, so the great arteries overlap and the vascular pedicle is narrow; stress-induced thymic involution narrows the superior mediastinum further. The heart below is oval and mildly enlarged, like an egg on its side hanging from a string.

findings.label: Pulmonary plethora (shunt vascularity)
findings.why: The pulmonary artery arises from the LV and pulmonary vascular resistance is low, so with the mixing lesions (atrial communication, VSD, PDA) pulmonary flow is high and large vessels reach the outer third of the lungs.

links.why: Antero-posterior great arteries (aorta anterior and to the right) give the narrow pedicle that is the signature of d-transposition.
High pulmonary flow fits transposition with mixing lesions; oligaemia would instead suggest tetralogy or transposition with pulmonary stenosis.

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; congenital heart disease); Perloff's Clinical Recognition of Congenital Heart Disease (newborn presentation, film evolution and management); ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines (adult follow-up after the arterial or atrial switch)
items.title: Transposition of the great arteries

candidates.label: Figure-3 sign of the aortic contour

items.concept: acyanotic congenital heart disease; aorta; secondary hypertension
items.explanation: Look first at the left upper mediastinal border (aortic knob), then along the lower edges of the posterior ribs. A '3' and bilateral rib notching in a hypertensive young adult is coarctation; on a barium swallow the same two bulges indent the oesophagus as a reversed 3 (the 'E' sign). Notching on one side only: right-sided when the coarctation is proximal to the left subclavian artery; left-sided when an aberrant right subclavian artery arises below the coarctation. Associated: upper limb hypertension, weak and delayed femoral pulses (radio-femoral delay), a systolic or continuous murmur over the back from the coarctation or the collaterals, and an ejection click when the aortic valve is bicuspid (about half or more of cases); ECG LV hypertrophy; echo (suprasternal view) shows a high-velocity jet with diastolic run-off, and CT or MR defines the anatomy. What would change the picture: a widened mediastinum without a waist suggests aneurysm or dissection; a large pulmonary artery with plethora suggests a shunt such as a PDA.

findings.label: Figure-3 sign of the aortic contour
findings.why: The upper bulge is the prestenotic arch with a dilated left subclavian artery, the notch is the coarctation itself and the lower bulge is post-stenotic dilatation of the descending aorta, so the left upper mediastinal border reads as a '3'.

findings.label: Inferior rib notching
findings.why: Intercostal arteries fed from the subclavian arteries (through the internal thoracic arteries) carry blood around the obstruction into the descending aorta. They enlarge, become tortuous and erode the inferior margins of the posterior ribs, usually ribs 3 to 8 on both sides; ribs 1 and 2 are spared because their intercostal arteries arise from the costocervical trunk, not the aorta.

links.why: The waist in the aortic contour is the coarctation, just distal to the left subclavian artery at the level of the ductus (ligamentum) arteriosus.
Notching shows a long-standing collateral circulation bypassing an aortic obstruction; it is rare before about 5 to 8 years of age, so a young child with coarctation may have none.

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; congenital heart disease; diseases of the aorta); Felson's Principles of Chest Roentgenology; ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines
items.title: Coarctation of the aorta

candidates.label: Double density at the right heart border

items.concept: pericardial disease; pericardial effusion; enlarged cardiac silhouette
items.explanation: Look first at the heart outline, then at the lungs: a big, smooth, flask-shaped silhouette with clear lung fields and normal upper-zone vessels points to fluid around a normal-sized heart; a silhouette that grows quickly on serial films without congestion also suggests effusion. Because the silhouette enlarges only after about 200-250 mL, a small but rapidly accumulating effusion can cause tamponade with a normal film. On the lateral film the epicardial fat pad sign (a band of fluid separating the epicardial from the pericardial fat) is specific. Associated: soft heart sounds; in tamponade raised JVP, hypotension and pulsus paradoxus; ECG with low QRS voltage and electrical alternans; echo confirms the effusion and looks for right atrial collapse (late diastole to early systole; more specific when it lasts more than a third of the cardiac cycle), early diastolic RV collapse, a plethoric IVC and exaggerated respiratory variation of mitral and tricuspid inflow. What would change the picture: venous congestion with an LV-shaped apex favours dilated cardiomyopathy; pericardial calcification with a normal-sized heart favours constriction.

findings.label: Water-bottle (flask-shaped) cardiac silhouette
findings.why: Fluid fills the pericardial sac, which hangs from the great vessels: the silhouette becomes large, globular and symmetric, wider at the base than at the narrow pedicle, with smooth sharp edges that efface the normal arcs (no visible left atrial appendage or pulmonary artery bulge). It needs at least about 200-250 mL of fluid.

findings.label: Left pleural effusion
findings.why: Pleural and pericardial fluid often share a cause (tuberculosis, malignancy, uraemia, hypothyroidism, inflammatory or post-pericardiotomy pericarditis), so a pleural effusion often accompanies a pericardial one.

links.why: A large, smooth, featureless silhouette with clear lungs is fluid around the heart rather than a dilated, failing ventricle.
A shared cause of pleural and pericardial fluid; tuberculosis is a leading cause of large effusions in Indonesia, with malignancy and uraemia.

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; pericardial diseases); Felson's Principles of Chest Roentgenology; ESC 2025 myocarditis and pericarditis guidelines; ESC 2015 pericardial diseases guidelines
items.title: Large pericardial effusion

candidates.label: Dilated ascending aorta (right upper mediastinal bulge)
Double density at the right heart border
Left ventricular enlargement (apex displaced down and out)

items.concept: valvular heart disease; aortic stenosis; post-stenotic dilatation
items.explanation: Look first at the heart size and the right upper mediastinum, then search the heart shadow for calcium. Pressure overload produces concentric hypertrophy, so the CTR stays normal (the apex may look rounded) until the LV fails; a normal-sized heart with a dilated ascending aorta and valve calcification fits AS. On the lateral film aortic valve calcium lies above and in front of a line from the carina to the anterior costophrenic angle, mitral annular calcium below and behind it. Associated: slow-rising, low-volume pulse, sustained apex beat, ejection systolic murmur radiating to the carotids, soft or single S2; ECG LV hypertrophy with strain; severity needs echo-Doppler (severe: Vmax 4 m/s or more, mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, AVA below 1.0 cm2). What would change the picture: an enlarged LV with a dilated aorta suggests aortic regurgitation; a '3' sign with rib notching suggests coarctation, which often coexists with a bicuspid valve.

findings.label: Dilated ascending aorta (right upper mediastinal bulge)
findings.why: The high-velocity jet through the stenotic valve strikes the ascending aorta (post-stenotic dilatation), and a bicuspid valve adds an intrinsic aortopathy. The ascending aorta then bulges to the right below the straight SVC line, between it and the right atrium.

findings.label: Aortic valve calcification
findings.why: Degenerative or bicuspid calcific disease deposits calcium in the cusps. It projects over the heart shadow near the midline at the level of the valve and is easier to see on the lateral film, fluoroscopy or CT.

links.why: Post-stenotic dilatation from the jet of a stenotic valve, and its size does not reflect the severity of the stenosis; aortic regurgitation also dilates the aorta but enlarges the LV.

Valve calcium in an adult with an ejection murmur strongly suggests calcific AS as the cause; aortic sclerosis can calcify without significant obstruction, so the film does not grade severity (on CT, a higher calcium score goes with more severe stenosis).

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; aortic valve disease); Felson's Principles of Chest Roentgenology; ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 valvular heart disease guidelines
items.title: Calcific aortic stenosis

candidates.label: Double density at the right heart border
Peripheral pruning of the pulmonary arteries

items.concept: acyanotic congenital heart disease; left-to-right shunt; increased pulmonary blood flow
items.explanation: Look first at the vascularity: large vessels reaching the periphery in all zones mean a left-to-right shunt. Then locate it: an ASD enlarges the right atrium (convex right heart border), the right ventricle (rounded, uplifted apex) and the pulmonary arteries but not the left atrium, and the aortic knob is normal or small (small on this film); a VSD or PDA also enlarges the left atrium and LV, and a PDA the aortic knob. Associated: wide, fixed splitting of S2, a pulmonary ejection murmur and, with a large shunt, a tricuspid flow rumble; ECG incomplete RBBB with right axis deviation (secundum) or left axis deviation (primum); echo shows the defect, RV volume overload and the shunt direction. Closure is recommended when there is RV volume overload without significant pulmonary vascular disease (PVR below 3 Wood units in the ESC 2020 guideline). What would change the picture: enlarged central arteries with peripheral pruning and dark outer lungs mean established pulmonary hypertension (Eisenmenger physiology if the shunt has reversed).

findings.label: Enlarged main pulmonary artery segment
findings.why: The atrial left-to-right shunt increases RV output (pulmonary flow often two to three times systemic), and the high flow dilates the pulmonary trunk, which bulges on the left heart border below the aortic knob.

findings.label: Enlarged hilar pulmonary arteries
findings.why: The same high flow enlarges the central pulmonary arteries at both hila, in the lung beside the heart: the right interlobar artery runs down lateral to the right heart border (the lucent bronchus intermedius between them) and the left pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus (on fluoroscopy they pulsate vigorously: the 'hilar dance').

findings.label: Pulmonary plethora (shunt vascularity)
findings.why: Increased pulmonary blood flow makes the vessels large and visible out to the lateral third of the lungs, in the upper and the lower zones alike (unlike upper lobe diversion). It becomes visible once pulmonary flow is roughly twice systemic flow.

findings.label: Cardiomegaly (CTR > 0.5)
findings.why: The shunt volume-loads the right atrium and right ventricle (CTR about 0.56 here): the right atrial border bulges convexly to the right and the enlarged RV rounds the apex and lifts it off the diaphragm, instead of the LV pattern of an apex displaced down and out. The left atrium decompresses through the defect, so it is not enlarged.

links.why: High pulmonary flow from the atrial left-to-right shunt dilates the pulmonary trunk.
Central arteries enlarge with flow; the peripheral arteries are large too (no pruning), so flow, not pressure, is the dominant problem.
Plethora marks a significant left-to-right shunt; with a normal left atrium and aortic knob the shunt is most likely at atrial level.
Right atrial and RV volume overload with a normal left atrium is the pattern of a pre-tricuspid shunt such as an ASD.

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; congenital heart disease in the adult); Perloff's Clinical Recognition of Congenital Heart Disease; ESC 2020 adult congenital heart disease guidelines
items.title: Secundum atrial septal defect

candidates.label: Double density at the right heart border
Peripheral pruning of the pulmonary arteries

items.explanation: Look first at the hila and compare them with the periphery: big central arteries that taper abruptly to a dark periphery mean pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension; big vessels all the way out mean a shunt (plethora); upper lobe diversion and septal lines point to post-capillary (left heart) PH. The RV enlarges as it fails (filling the retrosternal space on the lateral film), but the CTR can stay normal for a long time. The film cannot tell PAH from CTEPH or lung-disease PH; V/Q scan, CT and right heart catheterisation classify it. A normal film does not exclude PH: ESC/ERS 2022 defines PH as a mean pulmonary arterial pressure above 20 mmHg at right heart catheterisation (PAH: wedge 15 mmHg or less and PVR above 2 Wood units), and echo gives the probability (peak TR velocity above 2.8 m/s plus other signs). Associated: loud P2, left parasternal heave, TR murmur, raised JVP; ECG right axis deviation, RV hypertrophy, P pulmonale. What would change the picture: plethora means a shunt (ASD, VSD, PDA; pruning returns when Eisenmenger physiology develops); lobulated hila with normal peripheral vessels suggest lymphadenopathy (sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, lymphoma); a large left atrium with venous hypertension suggests mitral stenosis.

findings.label: Enlarged main pulmonary artery segment
findings.why: Raised pulmonary arterial pressure dilates the pulmonary trunk, so the segment between the aortic knob and the left atrial appendage bulges outward on the left heart border.

findings.label: Enlarged hilar pulmonary arteries
findings.why: The central pulmonary arteries dilate under high pressure, so both hila are large and arterial in shape: the right descending (interlobar) artery runs down lateral to the right heart border, and wider than about 16 mm it is abnormal; the left pulmonary artery arches large over the left main bronchus.

findings.label: Peripheral pruning of the pulmonary arteries
findings.why: Remodelling of the small pulmonary arteries (medial hypertrophy, intimal proliferation, plexiform lesions) narrows them, so the vessels taper abruptly beyond the hila and the outer lung fields look dark and empty.

links.why: Pressure overload of the pulmonary trunk in pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension.
Large central arteries with small peripheral ones is the pattern of high resistance; hila enlarged by lymph nodes would be lobulated with normal peripheral vessels.
Abrupt tapering reflects the raised small-artery resistance that defines PAH (PVR above 2 Wood units with a normal wedge pressure).

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; pulmonary hypertension); Felson's Principles of Chest Roentgenology; ESC/ERS 2022 pulmonary hypertension guidelines
items.title: Pulmonary arterial hypertension

items.concept: aortic disease; acute aortic syndrome; acute chest pain
items.explanation: Look first at the mediastinal width and the aortic contour, then at the knob for calcium and at the left base; also look for loss of the aortopulmonary window, displacement of the trachea or a nasogastric tube to the right and a left apical cap. Any of these in a patient with abrupt, tearing chest or back pain is suspicious, but the chest film is insensitive (in IRAD a widened mediastinum in about 60%, an abnormal aortic contour in about half and a normal film in about 1 in 8, 12-15%) and never excludes dissection: CT angiography (or TOE at the bedside when unstable) is the test (ESC 2024). Associated: pulse or blood pressure difference between the arms, a new aortic regurgitation murmur, neurological deficit; the ECG may be normal or show ischaemia when the flap involves a coronary ostium (usually the right), so a widened mediastinum must be imaged before any thrombolysis. What would change the picture: a '3' sign with rib notching suggests coarctation; a flask-shaped heart suggests effusion, which in a type A dissection may be haemopericardium (a surgical emergency).

findings.label: Widened superior mediastinum
findings.why: The dissected aorta enlarges (false lumen, wall haematoma, periaortic or mediastinal blood), so the superior mediastinum is wider than about 6 cm on an erect PA film (about 8 cm on a supine AP film; thresholds vary between sources), with a bulging ascending aorta and a large, ill-defined aortic knob.

findings.label: Calcium sign (intimal calcification displaced inward)
findings.why: Atherosclerotic calcium sits in the intima. When blood splits the media, the false lumen lies outside the intimal flap, so the calcium is separated from the outer aortic edge by more than about 6 mm (more than 10 mm is more specific).

findings.label: Left pleural effusion
findings.why: A left effusion can be blood leaking from the descending thoracic aorta (haemothorax) or a reactive exudate from the inflamed aortic wall.

links.why: An enlarged, dissected thoracic aorta with surrounding haematoma widens the mediastinum.
Intimal calcium separated from the outer wall is direct evidence of a thickened wall or a false lumen.
Blood or reactive fluid from a leaking descending thoracic aorta; a haemothorax marks a complicated dissection (possible rupture).

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; diseases of the aorta); Felson's Principles of Chest Roentgenology; ESC 2024 peripheral arterial and aortic diseases guidelines; ACC/AHA 2022 aortic disease guideline
items.title: Acute aortic dissection

items.concept: pericardial disease; constrictive pericarditis; right heart failure
items.explanation: Look first at the cardiac outline for a thin white rim and at the heart size: constriction usually has a normal or small heart, unlike a pericardial effusion or dilated cardiomyopathy. Calcification is seen in only a minority (roughly a quarter) of patients, so its absence does not exclude constriction. Associated: raised JVP with a prominent y descent and Kussmaul sign, pericardial knock, ascites and oedema out of proportion to lung congestion; ECG with low voltage, non-specific T-wave changes, often atrial fibrillation; echo shows a septal bounce, respiratory variation of mitral inflow, preserved or increased medial e' despite raised filling pressure (annulus paradoxus), often higher than lateral e' (annulus reversus), expiratory diastolic flow reversal in the hepatic veins and a dilated IVC; CT or MR shows pericardial thickening; catheterisation shows dip-and-plateau and discordant ventricular pressures with respiration. What would change the picture: the same right heart failure without pericardial calcium or thickening and with large atria suggests restrictive cardiomyopathy (for example amyloidosis); a large globular silhouette suggests effusion.

findings.label: Curvilinear pericardial calcification
findings.why: Chronic inflammation (tuberculosis is the leading cause in Indonesia and other endemic countries; also previous cardiac surgery, radiation and idiopathic or viral pericarditis) thickens and calcifies the pericardium. The calcium follows the heart outline, mainly over the right heart, the diaphragmatic surface and the atrioventricular grooves, and is best seen on the lateral film.

findings.label: Right pleural effusion
findings.why: Constriction raises systemic and pulmonary venous pressure (diastolic pressures equalise), so pleural effusions are common, often bilateral.

links.why: A calcified pericardium around a normal-sized heart in a patient with right heart failure is the classic film of constriction, although calcium alone does not prove constrictive physiology.
Effusion from the raised venous pressure of a heart that cannot fill; restrictive cardiomyopathy gives similar haemodynamics but no pericardial calcium.

items.source: Braunwald's Heart Disease (chest radiography; pericardial diseases); Felson's Principles of Chest Roentgenology; ESC 2025 myocarditis and pericarditis guidelines; ESC 2015 pericardial diseases guidelines
items.title: Constrictive pericarditis
